text: The first living things were single cells, far too small to see without a [[microscope|microscope]]. They lived in water, at least 3.5 billion years ago, when Earth was a very different planet, with no oxygen in the air and no plants on land. They were probably similar in some ways to today's [[bacteria|bacteria]] and other [[microbe|microbes]].

The oldest widely accepted [[fossil|fossils]] of life are stromatolites, layered rocks built by communities of microbes, found in Australia and about 3.5 billion years old. Some scientists think life began even earlier, over 4 billion years ago. Where and how life first appeared is one of the great open questions in science.

sec.t:
Stromatolites form when sticky mats of microbes trap sand and mud. The microbes grow up through each layer to reach sunlight, and over years they build mounds, layer on layer, like a pile of pancakes.

Fossil stromatolites about 3.5 billion years old have been found in the Pilbara region of Western Australia. Older signs of life have been claimed from rocks in [[@world-greenland|Greenland]] and Canada, but scientists still argue about them, because similar patterns can form without life.

India has ancient stromatolites too. Rocks near Udaipur and [[@chittorgarh|Chittorgarh]] in Rajasthan contain stromatolites well over a billion years old. Living ones still grow in Shark Bay, Australia, where the water is too salty for snails that would graze them away.

There are two leading ideas. Some scientists think life began at [[@deep-sea-vents|hydrothermal vents]] on the sea floor, where hot, mineral-rich water provides energy and chemicals. Others favour shallow pools on land that dried out and filled again, concentrating chemicals each time. In 1871, Charles Darwin wondered in a letter whether life might have started in a "warm little pond".

In 1952, Stanley Miller, a student working with Harold Urey at the University of Chicago, tried to copy early Earth in a glass flask. He used water, gases and electric sparks to act like [[@lightning|lightning]]. Within days, the water contained amino [[acid|acids]], building blocks of proteins. It was a major step, but no living thing appeared.

For billions of years, life stayed small. Some of those microbes, called cyanobacteria, learned to use sunlight to make food by [[@photosynthesis|photosynthesis]], giving off oxygen as waste. Around 2.4 billion years ago, oxygen began building up in the air, an event called the Great Oxidation.

That oxygen later made larger, more active life possible, including animals. It also changed the rocks. Iron dissolved in the oceans reacted with oxygen and settled on the sea floor as red, rust-coloured layers. Many of the world's big iron ore deposits, including some in India, are ancient banded rocks like these. Every breath you take depends on what those tiny cells started.

sec.h: तेज़ चक्र: हवा, पौधे और जानवर
sec.t:
चक्र का सबसे तेज़ हिस्सा रोज़ हमारे आस-पास होता है। [[@photosynthesis|प्रकाश संश्लेषण]] में पौधे और [[algae|शैवाल]] कार्बन डाइऑक्साइड और पानी लेते हैं और धूप की मदद से शक्कर बनाते हैं। इसी शक्कर से वे पत्तियाँ, लकड़ी और जड़ें बढ़ाते हैं।

जब कोई जानवर पौधा खाता है, तो कार्बन उसके शरीर में चला जाता है। हर बार साँस छोड़ते हुए तुम उसका कुछ हिस्सा कार्बन डाइऑक्साइड के रूप में हवा को लौटा देते हो। जब पौधे और जानवर मरते हैं, तो फफूँद और बैक्टीरिया उन्हें तोड़ते हैं और उनका कार्बन भी छोड़ देते हैं। उष्णकटिबंधीय जंगल में गिरा हुआ पत्ता कुछ ही हफ़्तों में ग़ायब हो सकता है।

कुछ कार्बन बहुत लंबे समय तक एक जगह टिका रहता है। करोड़ों साल पहले दबे दलदल के पौधे दबाव और गरमी से [[@oil-coal|कोयले और तेल]] में बदल गए। चूना पत्थर करोड़ों सालों तक कार्बन थामे रख सकता है।

धीरे-धीरे यह वापस आता है। बारिश चट्टानों को घिसती है और कार्बन को समुद्र तक ले जाती है। धरती की पपड़ी की खिसकती [[tectonic-plates|प्लेटें]] चट्टानों को ज़मीन में गहरे धकेल देती हैं, और [[@volcano|ज्वालामुखी]] उस कार्बन का कुछ हिस्सा गैस बनाकर फिर बाहर छोड़ देते हैं। यह धीमा चक्र लाखों साल लेता है, और इसने लंबे-लंबे दौरों में धरती की जलवायु को स्थिर रखने में मदद की है।

1958 में अमेरिकी वैज्ञानिक चार्ल्स डेविड कीलिंग ने [[@hawaii-islands|हवाई]] के एक ज्वालामुखी, मौना लोआ, पर कार्बन डाइऑक्साइड नापना शुरू किया। यह जगह शहरों और कारख़ानों से दूर थी, इसलिए वहाँ की हवा अच्छी तरह मिली-जुली थी।

उनका माप, जो आज तक जारी है, कीलिंग कर्व कहलाता है। यह हर साल टेढ़ा-मेढ़ा ऊपर-नीचे होता है, जैसे-जैसे उत्तरी जंगल बढ़ते और पत्ते गिराते हैं। पर साथ ही यह लगातार चढ़ता भी जा रहा है। लगभग 1750 से पहले हवा में कार्बन डाइऑक्साइड लगभग 280 पार्ट्स पर मिलियन थी, यानी हवा के हर दस लाख हिस्सों में 280 हिस्से। मई 2025 में मौना लोआ पर यह लगभग 430 नापी गई।

sec.h: आज यह क्यों मायने रखता है
sec.t:
कोयला, तेल और गैस जलाना उस कार्बन को, जो लाखों सालों से बंद था, बस दो-एक सदियों में हवा में पहुँचा देता है। जंगल काटने से और भी जुड़ता है। कार्बन डाइऑक्साइड एक [[greenhouse-gas|ग्रीनहाउस गैस]] है, जो गरमी को फँसाती है, इसलिए इसका बढ़ना धरती को गरम कर रहा है।

जंगल, मिट्टी और समुद्र इसका कुछ अतिरिक्त हिस्सा सोख लेते हैं, और इससे मदद मिलती है। सुंदरबन के [[@mangroves|मैंग्रोव]] जैसी तटीय जगहें अपनी कीचड़ भरी मिट्टी में भारी मात्रा में कार्बन जमा रखती हैं। इन्हें बचाना, पेड़ लगाना और कम ईंधन जलाना, सब ज़्यादा कार्बन को हवा से दूर रखने में मदद करते हैं।

text: Hail needs a very tall storm cloud with powerful winds rushing upwards inside it. India makes those clouds best in March, April and May, just before the [[@monsoon|monsoon]]. The ground gets baking hot, while the air several kilometres up is still cold and dry.

Hot air near the ground rises fast, like a bubble in a pot of boiling dal. It carries water droplets high into the cloud, where it is well below freezing. The droplets freeze onto tiny bits of ice and grow. Strong upward winds keep tossing them back up, so they keep growing. When a stone gets too heavy for the wind to hold, it falls.

sec.t:
The clouds behind hail are cumulonimbus clouds, the giants that also make [[@thunderstorms|thunderstorms]]. Some reach more than 10 km up, as high as passenger jets fly. Inside, the rising air can move faster than a car on a highway.

A hailstone starts as a small seed, maybe a frozen raindrop or a grain of dust. Super-cooled water, which is liquid even below 0 °C, freezes onto it the moment they touch. Each trip up and down adds another coat. That is why a cut hailstone often shows rings, like the inside of an onion.

Most hail is the size of a pea or a marble. The heaviest ever weighed, about 1 kg, fell on Gopalganj in Bangladesh in 1986. The largest in the United States was 20 cm across, as wide as a dinner plate, in Vivian, South Dakota, in 2010.

The timing is cruel for farmers. March and April are when [[@wheat-bread|wheat]] stands ripe in north Indian fields, mangoes hang on trees and grapes are ready in Nashik. Ten minutes of hail can flatten a crop that took months to grow. In early 2014, hailstorms across Maharashtra and nearby states damaged crops on a huge scale.

Hail can be dangerous for people and animals too. On 30 April 1888, a storm in Moradabad killed about 246 people. It is still listed as the deadliest hailstorm ever recorded.

Hailstorms are small and short, which makes them hard to forecast. A storm can grow from a few puffy clouds to a hail-maker in less than an hour. The [[@imd|India Meteorological Department]] watches for them with Doppler radar, which can spot rain and ice moving inside a cloud.

When the signs look strong, it sends out "nowcasts", warnings for the next few hours. Farmers can't move a field of wheat indoors. They can, though, bring animals under cover, pick ripe fruit early and park tractors in a shed.

In the United States, the worst hail falls on the Great Plains, in states such as Texas, Colorado and Nebraska. Hail there damages billions of dollars' worth of cars, roofs and crops in a bad year. The cause is the same as in India: hot ground below, cold dry air above, and a giant cloud in between.

text: The ocean is Earth's giant heat battery. Water takes a lot of energy to warm up and gives that energy back slowly. Because the ocean covers about 71% of the planet, it soaks up sunlight in summer and in the tropics, then releases warmth in winter and carries it towards the poles.

Ocean currents move that heat around like a slow conveyor belt. Water [[evaporation|evaporating]] from warm seas feeds clouds and rain, including India's [[@monsoon|monsoon]]. The ocean also swallows [[carbon-dioxide|carbon dioxide]] from the air. Without it, summers would be hotter, winters colder and the planet warming faster.

sec.t:
Sit on a beach at noon and the sand burns your feet, while the water stays cool. At night the sand is cold and the water feels warm. Water simply needs more energy than sand or air to change its temperature.

That is why coastal cities have gentler weather. Mumbai mostly stays between about 16°C and 35°C all year. Delhi, hundreds of kilometres from the nearest sea, can swing from about 45°C in May to under 5°C on a January morning. In the USA, San Francisco and Kansas City show the same pattern: one is cooled by the Pacific, the other bakes and freezes in the middle of the continent.

India's summer rain is an ocean story. In April and May, the land heats up faster than the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal. Hot air rises over the land, and moist air from the sea flows in to replace it. That wet sea air brings the [[monsoon|monsoon]].

The ocean far away matters too. Every few years, a stretch of the Pacific near South America becomes unusually warm. This is [[@el-nino|El Niño]]. It shifts winds and rain around the globe, and in many El Niño years India's monsoon is weaker than normal. Weather forecasters in Pune and in Maryland watch Pacific temperatures for clues about the coming season.

Warm sea water is the energy source for [[tropical|tropical]] [[cyclone|cyclones]]. A cyclone needs sea surface temperatures of roughly 26°C or more. As water evaporates, it releases heat high in the clouds, which powers the spinning winds. The Bay of Bengal, often very warm, produces many of the [[@cyclones-india|cyclones]] that hit Odisha, Andhra Pradesh and Bangladesh. The same process drives [[@hurricanes|hurricanes]] that reach Florida and Texas.

Since the 1970s, the ocean has soaked up more than 90% of the extra heat trapped by [[greenhouse-gas|greenhouse gases]]. It has also absorbed about a quarter of the carbon dioxide people release each year. That has slowed warming on land.

But it comes at a cost. Warmer water expands, so sea levels rise. Heatwaves in the sea bleach [[@coral-reefs|coral]] reefs. When carbon dioxide dissolves in water, it makes the water slightly more acidic, which makes it harder for shellfish and corals to build shells. The heat the ocean has already stored will keep warming the planet for decades, even if emissions fall. Scientists measure all this using about 4,000 floating robots, called Argo floats, which drift and dive across every ocean.

text: Flowers are colourful because they are advertising. Most plants cannot move, so they need animals to carry [[pollen|pollen]] from one flower to another. Bright petals tell bees, [[@butterflies-life|butterflies]], birds and even bats: food here. The reward is usually sweet [[nectar|nectar]], or extra pollen to eat.

Each colour comes from chemicals in the petals called [[pigment|pigments]]. Different animals see colours differently, so flowers have [[evolve|evolved]] colours that suit their favourite visitors. Grass and many trees, which use the wind to carry pollen, do not bother with bright flowers at all.

d.try: Spend fifteen minutes watching one flowering plant in a garden, park or balcony pot. Note the flower colour and every visitor you see, from bees and butterflies to ants or birds. Then watch a flower of a different colour. Do the visitors change?
myth: Flowers are colourful to make the world look pretty for people.
Flower colours evolved long before humans existed. They are signals to animals, mostly insects and birds, that carry pollen from flower to flower. People simply enjoy the result.

sec.t:
Reds, purples and many blues come from pigments called anthocyanins. The same family of chemicals colours red cabbage, jamun and blueberries. Yellows and oranges usually come from carotenoids, also found in carrots and marigolds. White petals often have almost no pigment. They look white because air pockets inside scatter light, the way foam on a wave looks white.

Some flowers change colour with conditions. Hydrangeas grown in acidic soil tend to be blue. In less acidic soil, the same plant often turns pink. Gardeners sometimes add things to the soil to shift the shade.

Many red flowers are pollinated by birds. In the Americas, [[@hummingbirds|hummingbirds]] hover at red flowers with long tubes, like trumpet vines. In India, sunbirds visit red and orange flowers such as the flame of the forest, or palash, whose blossoms turn whole hillsides orange in spring.

Birds see red well and have little sense of smell. So bird flowers tend to be bright, tube-shaped and scentless. Bee flowers are more often blue, purple or yellow and sweet-smelling. Moths, which fly at night, prefer white or pale flowers with strong scents, like jasmine and raat ki rani, the night-blooming jessamine.

Not every flower plays fair. Some orchids look a bit like female bees or wasps, and males try to visit them. Rafflesia, a giant flower from Southeast Asian forests, is reddish brown and smells of rotting meat. It attracts flies that normally lay eggs on dead animals.

Colour can also change after [[pollination|pollination]]. Some lantana flowers start yellow and shift to orange or red once they have been visited. Insects learn that the newer colour means no more nectar, and skip those blooms.

In the Western Ghats, a shrub called neelakurinji covers the hills near Munnar in Kerala with blue-purple flowers only once every 12 years. The last mass flowering in Munnar was in 2018, and the next is expected around 2030. Tourists travel from all over India to see it. For the bees, it is a once-in-a-dozen-years feast. After flowering, the shrubs set seed and die, and the 12-year countdown starts again.

Flowering plants first appeared during the age of dinosaurs, more than 100 million years ago. Their bright colours spread alongside the insects that visited them, one of the longest partnerships in the living world.

text: Look closely at a house gecko's toes and you'll see rows of soft ridges underneath, like the gills of a mushroom. Each ridge is covered in hundreds of thousands of tiny hairs called setae. And each of those hairs splits at its tip into hundreds of even smaller pads, each about 200 nanometres wide. You could line up hundreds of them across the width of one human hair.

These pads get so close to a wall that the molecules in the pads and the molecules in the wall pull on each other. This pull, called the van der Waals force, is extremely weak for one pad. But a gecko has millions of them, and together they are strong enough to hold it on a ceiling.

sec.t:
For thousands of years people wondered about geckos. The Greek thinker Aristotle wrote about them climbing trees upside down more than 2,300 years ago. Later, people guessed suction cups, sticky liquid or tiny hooks.

In 2000, a team led by the American [[biologist|biologist]] Kellar Autumn finally measured the grip of a single gecko hair. It turned out that the hairs worked best dry, with no glue at all. The force between [[molecule|molecules]] was enough. Their calculations suggested that if every hair on a tokay gecko's feet gripped at once, the animal could in theory hold up around 130 kilograms, about as much as two grown men.

sec.h: Letting go is the clever part

sec.t:
In India, the house gecko or chhipkali is a familiar evening visitor, hunting insects around tube lights. Like many geckos, it is [[@nocturnal-animals|nocturnal]], active at night. The bigger tokay gecko of the Northeast and Southeast Asia is famous for its loud "to-kay" call.

There are more than 2,000 [[species|species]] of gecko, living on every continent except Antarctica. Not all can climb. About 60% have sticky toe pads, and some, like the leopard gecko kept as a pet, have none at all. Scientists think toe pads [[evolve|evolved]] several separate times in different gecko families.

Engineers love geckos. Stanford University built a climbing robot called Stickybot that used gecko-style rubber feet. NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory has tested gecko-inspired grippers to grab objects in space, where suction cups are useless because there is no air.

There is even gecko tape, which sticks without glue and can be peeled off and reused, a bit like [[@velcro|Velcro]] but smooth. Geckos are not the only animals using tiny hairs. Some spiders and beetles grip walls in a similar way. So when a household [[@lizards|lizard]] stalks a spider across your ceiling at night, both hunter and hunted may be hanging on by the same trick.

text: A kite flies because wind pushes on it at an angle while the string holds it back. The kite is tilted, so the moving air pushes it up as well as backwards. That upward push is called lift. The backward push is drag.

The string is the secret ingredient. It stops the wind from simply blowing the kite away, so the air has to flow over and under it. When lift, drag, the kite's weight and the pull of the string balance each other, the kite hangs in the sky. On a breezy day over a cricket ground, that balance can hold for hours.

sec.h: Four forces in a tug of war
sec.t:
Every kite is in a constant four-way tug of war. [[gravity|Gravity]] pulls it down. Lift pushes it up. Drag pushes it downwind. The string pulls it towards your hand.

Tilt matters most. This tilt is called the angle of attack. Too flat, and the wind slides past without lifting much. Too steep, and the kite acts like a wall, catching plenty of drag but little lift. The bridle, the little loop of string where the line joins the kite, sets that angle. Moving the knot a few centimetres can turn a sulky kite into a soaring one.

People in China were flying kites more than 2,000 years ago, at first perhaps made of wood or silk. Kites spread across Asia, where they were used for signalling, fishing and festivals. In Gujarat, the skies over Ahmedabad fill on 14 January for Uttarayan, when fliers try to cut each other's lines with glass-coated string called manja.

In America, [[@benjamin-franklin|Benjamin Franklin]] flew his famous kite into a thunderstorm in 1752 to show that lightning is electricity. He was lucky to survive. Nobody should ever try it.

Kites carried science upwards long before planes or balloons were reliable. From 1898, the US Weather Bureau flew kites carrying instruments to measure air temperature and wind. In 1919 a chain of kites over Germany climbed to about 9,740 m, higher than Mount Everest.

In 1899 the [[@wright-brothers|Wright brothers]] tested their idea of twisting wings on a large kite before building their first glider. And in December 1901, Guglielmo Marconi used a kite in Newfoundland to lift a long wire aerial. It picked up the first radio signal sent across the Atlantic, the letter S in Morse code from England. Those three faint clicks had travelled about 3,500 km, and the [[@radio-invented|invention of radio]] suddenly looked like it could connect whole continents.

Kites still work hard. Kitesurfers on the sea are dragged along at speeds faster than a car in town traffic. Engineers are testing huge kites that fly in loops and pull a cable to make electricity from strong winds high above the ground.

A kite and an airliner use the same basic science of tilted surfaces in moving air. The difference is that a plane makes its own wind by racing forward with engines, which is how [[@airplanes-fly|aeroplanes stay up]] without anyone holding a string.

text: सुलेख सुंदर लिखावट की कला है। अंग्रेज़ी में इसे कैलिग्राफ़ी कहते हैं, जो दो यूनानी शब्दों से बना है: *कैलोस*, यानी सुंदरता, और *ग्राफ़ीन*, यानी लिखना। सुलेखक हर अक्षर को ब्रश या ख़ास तरह से कटी कलम से बड़े ध्यान से गढ़ता है, ताकि लिखावट पढ़ने के साथ-साथ निहारने की चीज़ भी बन जाए।

लिखने वाली लगभग हर संस्कृति में सुलेख की कोई न कोई परंपरा है। [[@chinese-characters|चीनी और जापानी कलाकार]] नरम ब्रश इस्तेमाल करते हैं। [[@arabic-script|अरबी और फ़ारसी लिखने वाले]] सरकंडे की कलम चलाते हैं। [[medieval|मध्यकाल]] के यूरोपीय भिक्षु पंख की कलम से लिखते थे, और भारतीय लिपिकार ताड़ के पत्तों और कागज़ पर लिखते थे। सुलेख से धर्मग्रंथ, मस्जिदें, मंदिर, शादी के कार्ड और प्रमाणपत्र सजाए जाते हैं।

sec.t:
चीन में सुलेख 2,000 से भी ज़्यादा साल से सबसे सम्मानित कलाओं में गिना जाता रहा है। सुलेखक स्याही की ठोस बट्टी को पत्थर पर ज़रा-से पानी के साथ घिसकर ताज़ी स्याही बनाता है, फिर नरम, नुकीले ब्रश से कागज़ या रेशम पर लिखता है।

ज़्यादा दबाने पर रेखा मोटी बनती है, और ब्रश उठाने पर पतली। हर अक्षर में रेखाएँ खींचने का एक तय क्रम होता है, जिसे बच्चे स्कूल में सीखते हैं, ठीक वैसे जैसे हम "क" लिखना सीखते समय पहले कौन सी लकीर खींचें, यह सीखते हैं। लगभग 1,700 साल पहले हुए वांग शीझी जैसे महान सुलेखक चित्रकारों जितने मशहूर थे।

भारत में बहुत-सी [[script|लिपियाँ]] हैं, देवनागरी और [[@bengali-language|बांग्ला]] से लेकर तमिल और [[@punjabi-gurmukhi|गुरमुखी]] तक। हर लिपि की अपनी सुलेख परंपरा है, जिसके बारे में [[@scripts-india|भारत में कितनी लिपियाँ चलती हैं?]] में और जान सकते हो। सदियों तक दक्षिण भारत के लिपिकार सूखे ताड़-पत्रों पर धातु की नुकीली सुई से अक्षर खुरचते थे, फिर उन पर कालिख या दीये का काजल मलते थे, ताकि अक्षर गहरे दिखें।

ओड़िया और [[@malayalam|मलयालम]] जैसी गोल-मटोल लिपियाँ शायद कुछ हद तक इसलिए घुमावदार हुईं क्योंकि पत्ते की नसों के साथ-साथ खींची सीधी लकीर ताड़-पत्र को चीर देती। आज भारतीय सुलेखक कई लिपियों में कलाकृतियाँ, लोगो और फ़िल्मों के टाइटल बनाते हैं।

मध्यकालीन यूरोप में, छपाई आने से पहले, किताबें हाथ से नकल की जाती थीं, अक्सर भिक्षुओं के हाथों। वे हंस के पंखों से कटी कलमें इस्तेमाल करते थे और जानवरों की खाल से बने चर्मपत्र पर लिखते थे।

लगभग 800 ईस्वी में आयरलैंड या स्कॉटलैंड में बनी *बुक ऑफ़ केल्स* इनमें सबसे मशहूर है। इसमें लैटिन में चारों गॉस्पेल (ईसा मसीह के जीवन की कथाएँ) हैं, जिन्हें घूमते-लिपटते नमूनों, जानवरों और बड़े-बड़े रंगे हुए पहले अक्षरों से सजाया गया है। यह आज डबलिन के ट्रिनिटी कॉलेज में रखी है। 1400 के दशक में [[@printing-press|छापाख़ाना]] आने के बाद हाथ से लिखी किताबें धीरे-धीरे दुर्लभ हो गईं।

1970 के दशक में स्टीव जॉब्स नाम के एक अमेरिकी नौजवान ने कॉलेज छोड़ दिया, पर वहाँ सुलेख की एक क्लास में जाते रहे। बरसों बाद एक मशहूर भाषण में उन्होंने कहा कि उसी क्लास ने 1984 के पहले ऐपल मैकिंटॉश के बहुत-से टाइपफ़ेस को आकार दिया। उस समय ज़्यादातर कंप्यूटरों में बस एक ही, चौकोर-सा फ़ॉन्ट होता था।

फ़ोन या लैपटॉप पर दिखने वाला हर फ़ॉन्ट किसी ने अक्षरों के आकार के बारे में सोचकर बनाया है, और बहुत-से टाइप डिज़ाइनर शुरुआत सुलेख सीखकर करते हैं। तुम्हारी स्क्रीन के अक्षर एक तरह का [[@design-everyday|रोज़मर्रा का डिज़ाइन]] हैं, जिनकी जड़ें हज़ारों साल गहरी हैं।

text: Courage is doing something good or necessary even though it scares you. A firefighter running into smoke has it. So does a child who tells a teacher that a classmate is being bullied, knowing the bully might turn on them next.

The key word is *even though*. Courage doesn't mean the [[@fear|fear]] disappears. Your heart still races and your hands still sweat. Courage is the part of you that decides what to do anyway. Without fear there would be nothing to be brave about.

sec.t:
People often split courage into two kinds. Physical courage means facing danger to your body: climbing a dangerous mountain, pulling someone out of a flooded river, or jumping into the ring for your first boxing match.

Moral courage means standing up for what is right when it could cost you friends, money or comfort. In 1955, [[@rosa-parks|Rosa Parks]] refused to give up her bus seat to a white passenger in Montgomery, Alabama. She was arrested, but her quiet act helped spark the American civil rights movement. In Pakistan, [[@malala|Malala Yousafzai]] spoke out for girls' schooling even after she was attacked for it.

When something frightens you, a small almond-shaped part of your brain called the [[amygdala|amygdala]] raises the alarm. Your heart pumps faster, your breathing speeds up and your muscles get ready to run.

Other parts of the brain, toward the front, can weigh that alarm against what you want to do. In a 2010 experiment in Israel, scientists asked people who were afraid of snakes to pull a live snake closer on a moving belt. When people chose to bring it nearer despite feeling scared, a region in the front of their brain became more active. The fear was still there. Something else was overruling it.

Practice helps too. Firefighters, soldiers and astronauts rehearse frightening moments again and again, in drills and simulators, until their hands know what to do. The fear doesn't vanish, but it gets smaller and stops freezing them. The same thing happens when a shy child gives a second, third and fourth speech in class. Each time, the alarm rings a little more quietly.

{{story:everest-first}}

On 5 September 1986, armed men took over Pan Am Flight 73 on the ground at Karachi airport. Neerja Bhanot, a 22-year-old flight attendant from Mumbai, warned the pilots. Over the next long hours she helped keep passengers calm and hid passports so the hijackers could not pick out Americans.

When the attackers began shooting, she opened the emergency doors and helped people escape. She was killed while helping children get out. India awarded her the Ashoka Chakra, its highest award for bravery away from war. Pakistan and the USA honoured her too.

Most acts of courage never make the news. Owning up to a mistake takes courage, especially when nobody saw you make it and you could easily stay quiet. So does sitting with a new student at lunch, or trying a sport you're bad at while others watch.

The ancient Greek thinker Aristotle said courage sits between two faults. Too little, and you are a coward who runs from every risk. Too much, and you are reckless, taking silly risks for no good reason. A brave person, he thought, fears the right things for the right reasons.

India has given National Bravery Awards to children since 1957, and in the USA the Carnegie Hero Fund has honoured ordinary rescuers since 1904. Many winners say the same thing afterwards: they were terrified, and they did it anyway.

text: Being fair means treating people in a way that they, and others watching, can accept as right. It often means following the same rules for everyone, sharing in a way that makes sense, and not cheating or playing favourites.

But fairness is tricky, because there is more than one kind. Sometimes fair means equal, like each player getting the same number of turns. Sometimes it means giving according to need, like more water for the thirsty runner. Sometimes it means giving according to effort, like more marks for the better answer. People argue about which kind fits which situation, and those arguments are one of the oldest conversations in human history.

st.prompt: Three children must share 12 sweets. One child has not eaten all day. What is the fair way to split them?

options.t: People will disagree, and both "equal shares" and "more for the hungry child" have good reasons
Exactly four each, there is no other fair answer
Whoever asks first gets the most

st.reveal: Four each is equal. Giving the hungry child more looks at need. Both are serious ideas of fairness, and grown-ups argue about the same question when they talk about taxes, school places and healthcare. Talking it through openly is part of being fair.

myth: Being fair always means giving everyone exactly the same.

Sometimes equal is fair, like everyone getting one vote. But a ramp for a wheelchair user or glasses for someone who can't see the board give different people different things so they can take part equally. Many people call this kind of fairness equity.
facts: Sarah Brosnan and Frans de Waal, published 2003

sec.t:
In 2003, scientists Sarah Brosnan and Frans de Waal ran a famous experiment with capuchin monkeys. Each monkey handed a small stone to a researcher and got a piece of cucumber in return. They were perfectly happy with the deal.

Then one monkey started getting grapes, which capuchins like much more. Its neighbour, still getting cucumber, often refused the food or even threw it back. The video went around the world. Scientists still debate exactly what the monkeys were thinking, but many see it as a sign that a sense of fairness goes deep, perhaps older than humans.

Games are a good place to see fairness at work. Both teams follow the same [[@why-rules|rules]], the toss decides who goes first, and an umpire makes the calls. When fans feel an umpire has been unfair, they get very angry, which shows how much fairness matters to people.

Sport has also worked hard to be fairer. Technology like the third umpire in cricket and video review in football helps catch mistakes. Anti-doping tests try to stop athletes from cheating with drugs. Each of these exists because people wanted results they could trust.

sec.h: Equal, or what each person needs?
sec.t:
Laws in many countries promise equal treatment. Article 14 of India's Constitution says everyone is equal before the law, and the US Constitution's 14th Amendment makes a similar promise.

But [[@equality|equality]] can mean different things. If two children are watching a cricket match over a wall and one is much shorter, giving them the same-sized box to stand on may still leave one unable to see. Giving the shorter child a taller box treats them differently, so both can see. Governments in India and the United States have tried policies to help groups who were treated unfairly in the past. People disagree, sometimes strongly, about how well these policies work and how long they should last.

The American thinker John Rawls, in a book published in 1971, suggested a clever test. Picture yourself designing the rules for a society without knowing who you will be in it: rich or poor, healthy or ill, from a big city or a small village. He called this the veil of ignorance.

If you didn't know where you'd end up, you'd probably want rules that are decent to everyone. You can try the same test at home. When you make a rule for your siblings, ask whether you'd still like it if you were the one on the other side.

text: Rules let people who don't know each other trust what will happen next. When you stop at a red light, you are counting on the driver coming the other way to stop too. When you bat in a match, you trust that the bowler can't suddenly throw from two metres away.

Without rules, every shared thing would turn into an argument: roads, playgrounds, money, even a queue at the canteen. Groups of people, from families to whole countries, make rules so they can live and work together without fighting over every small decision. The best rules feel fair to most people, and can be changed when they stop working.

st.reveal: On the day called Dagen H, crashes actually fell for a while, because drivers were nervous and paid close attention. After a couple of years things went back to normal. A big rule change worked because everyone switched at the same moment.

Many rules make things possible. Traffic rules let millions of strangers share roads, and game rules are the reason a game exists at all. Without agreed rules, cricket is just people hitting a ball.

sec.t:
Rulers have tried to write rules down for a very long time. Around 1750 BCE, King Hammurabi of Babylon had about 280 laws carved on a black stone pillar more than two metres tall. You can still see it in the Louvre in Paris. The [[@hammurabi|Code of Hammurabi]] covered things like debts, farming and building houses safely.

In India, the emperor [[@ashoka|Ashoka]] had his messages carved on rocks and pillars across his [[empire|empire]] in the 3rd century BCE. They asked people to respect parents, be kind to animals and treat other faiths with respect. Writing rules where everyone can read them means a ruler cannot simply change them in secret.

A game is really a set of rules. The oldest known written laws of cricket date from 1744. The Marylebone Cricket Club in London drew up its own code in 1788, and the club still updates it. Football, chess and carrom all work because both sides agree on what counts.

Games also show why people need referees and umpires. Everyone might know the rules, but someone still has to decide, quickly and calmly, whether the ball crossed the line. In the same way, countries have courts and judges to settle arguments about laws.

Some people follow rules because they fear punishment. But most of the time, people follow them because they see the point. Researchers who study cooperation, including mathematicians working on [[@game-theory|game theory]], find that groups do best when most people play fair and cheats are spotted.

Small children start to notice unfair rules very early. Ask any eight-year-old what happens when one sibling gets a bigger slice of cake. Our sense of [[@fairness|fairness]] is one reason good rules last, and unfair ones get challenged.

Rules are made by people, so they can be wrong. For many years, laws in India and the United States treated people unequally because of caste, race or being a woman. People protested, argued in courts and voted, and many of those laws were changed. Some rules simply go out of date. Old laws in some places once banned things that nobody worries about now, and lawmakers sometimes spend whole sessions clearing away rules that no one has used in a century. Other rules arrive with new inventions. There were no laws about seat belts before cars, and none about online privacy before the internet. A good rule book includes a way to rewrite itself.

text: A lottery is hard to win because there are a staggering number of possible tickets, and only one is the jackpot winner. In the US Powerball game, you choose 5 numbers from 1 to 69 and then a special red ball from 1 to 26. There are 292,201,338 different ways to fill in that ticket.

Buy one ticket and your chance of the jackpot is 1 in 292,201,338. That is about the same as flipping a coin and getting heads 28 times in a row. Most people flipping a coin never get past eight or nine heads in a row.
Lotteries work because millions of people play. Almost all of them lose a little, so that one person can win a lot.

st.prompt: In a lottery, the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 come up. How likely was that compared with any other set of six numbers?

options.t: Exactly as likely as any other set
Much less likely, because it is a pattern

st.reveal: The balls don't know they are in a pattern. Every set of numbers has the same tiny chance. Patterns only feel special because our brains notice them.

d.try: Flip a coin and count how many heads you get in a row before the first tails. Try it ten times and write down your best streak. Then work out what a 28-head streak would mean, by doubling 1 twenty-eight times on a calculator.
myth: Numbers that haven't come up for a long time are "due" to appear soon.
Every draw starts fresh. The machine has no memory, so a number that hasn't appeared in months has exactly the same chance as one that came up last week. This mistake is called the gambler's fallacy.

sec.t:
Here is how mathematicians count. For the first white ball there are 69 choices. Then 68 are left, then 67, then 66, then 65. Multiply them and you get 1,348,621,560.

But order doesn't matter in Powerball. Drawing 7 then 12 is the same as 12 then 7. Any group of five balls can be arranged in 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 120 orders. So divide by 120 and you get 11,238,513 different groups of five.

Now the red Powerball. There are 26 of those, so multiply by 26: 11,238,513 × 26 = 292,201,338. That is where the famous number comes from. The same method works for any lottery: count the choices, then divide out the orders that don't matter. It is a counting trick at the heart of [[@probability|probability]].

Numbers this size are hard to feel, which is why [[@big-numbers|big numbers]] trick us. So try these.

If you bought one Powerball ticket every week, you would expect to wait about 5.6 million years for a jackpot. That is longer than humans have existed.

Lay 292 million lottery tickets end to end, about 10 cm each, and the line would stretch more than 29,000 km. That is roughly three-quarters of the way around the Earth. Only one ticket in that line is the winner.

The US weather service puts the chance of being struck by lightning in a single year at roughly 1 in a million. A jackpot is hundreds of times less likely.

{{story:lightning}}

Lotteries take in far more money than they pay out. In most big US lotteries, only about half of the money from ticket sales comes back as prizes. The rest goes to running costs and to the state, which often spends it on schools or other services.

In India, lotteries are banned in many states and run by the government in others. [[@kerala|Kerala]] started its state lottery in 1967 and it is now hugely popular there. The maths is the same everywhere: on average, players lose money.

The biggest single Powerball prize so far was about $2.04 billion, won by one ticket in California in 2022.

People have all kinds of lottery strategies. Some pick birthdays. Some avoid numbers that won recently. None of this changes the odds. Every ticket has exactly the same chance.

Birthdays can make one thing worse, though. Lots of people pick numbers from 1 to 31. If those numbers win, the prize is more likely to be split among many winners. Random picks avoid that, but they won't make you more likely to win. And buying ten tickets instead of one? Your chance goes from 1 in 292 million to about 1 in 29 million. Still tiny.

And the strangest part? Some [[probability|probability]] puzzles fool even professional mathematicians, like the game-show riddle in [[@puzzle-monty-hall|the Monty Hall problem]].

The show started on the children's channel Pogo in 2008. It was made by Green Gold Animation in [[@hyderabad|Hyderabad]], a studio founded by Rajiv Chilaka. Simple stories, catchy songs, free TV and cheap toys and school bags helped it spread to millions of homes, from big cities to small towns.

sec.h: A hero borrowed from an epic

sec.t:
Bheem's best friend is Chutki, a clever girl whose mother makes the laddoos. There's Raju, a small boy who wants to be brave like Bheem, and Jaggu, a talking monkey. Kalia is the bully, always trying to beat Bheem, with his two sidekicks, the twins Dholu and Bholu.

The kingdom is ruled by Raja Indravarma, and his daughter, Princess Indumati, is one of Bheem's friends. The characters are simple and easy to tell apart, which helps very young children follow along. Each has one clear trait: Bheem is brave, Chutki is smart, Raju is eager, and Kalia is jealous. Episodes are short, usually around ten minutes, with a problem, a chase and a happy ending.

Before Chhota Bheem, most cartoons on Indian TV came from the USA or Japan. They were fun, but set in faraway cities with unfamiliar food and festivals. Chhota Bheem showed village fairs, Diwali, Holi, and plates of [[@sweets-india|Indian sweets]].

The show was dubbed into several Indian languages, so children could watch in Tamil, Telugu and others as well as Hindi. Pogo was part of the basic cable package in many homes, so families didn't need to pay extra to watch.

sec.h: From a small studio to a big brand
sec.t:
Rajiv Chilaka founded Green Gold Animation in Hyderabad in 2001. For years the company struggled. Like many [[@indian-animation|Indian studios]], it did [[@animation-how|animation]] work for others while trying to sell its own ideas.

Once Chhota Bheem took off, the characters appeared everywhere: on lunchboxes, T-shirts, toys and books. Several [[@childrens-films-india|feature films]] came out in cinemas. Studios across India took note that a home-grown character could earn money, and more Indian cartoons followed. Green Gold went on to create other series, and Bheem himself starred in longer TV specials and adventures set far beyond Dholakpur.

In 2019, Netflix released Mighty Little Bheem, a spin-off about Bheem as a toddler. It has almost no dialogue, so children anywhere can follow the jokes. The baby Bheem crawls around causing chaos with his superhuman strength.

Because it needs no translation, the show found fans in many countries. A cartoon born in Hyderabad, about a boy from an imaginary Indian village, was being watched by toddlers in many countries outside India. Few Indian cartoons had travelled so far.

text: The Republic Day parade is India's biggest national ceremony. It takes place every 26 January on Kartavya Path, the long, tree-lined avenue in [[@delhi|New Delhi]] that runs from the President's house towards India Gate.

The President unfurls the national flag, the national anthem plays, and a 21-gun salute booms out. Then the parade begins. Soldiers, sailors and airmen march in step. Tanks, missiles and camels roll and stride past. States send decorated floats, called tableaux. Schoolchildren dance. It ends with fighter jets roaring overhead. The whole show lasts about two hours, and millions more watch it on television.

Before the parade starts, the Prime Minister lays a wreath at the National War Memorial near India Gate, honouring soldiers who died for the country. Then the President arrives, escorted by the President's Bodyguard, a regiment of tall horsemen in red coats. Raised in 1773, it is the oldest regiment in the Indian Army.

The last British soldiers left that day
It is the day the national flag was designed

st.reveal: Independence came in 1947, but India was still using British-era laws. On 26 January 1950 its own Constitution began, and India became a republic with an elected head of state instead of a king.

sec.t:
The first parade, in 1950, was held at a stadium. Since 1955 it has used the broad avenue then called Rajpath, renamed Kartavya Path in 2022.

Each contingent marches past the President, who stands on a stage and takes their salute. There are regiments from every corner of the country, police and paramilitary forces, and the Border Security Force's camel riders in bright turbans. Military bands play as they walk, and each regiment has its own marching tune. Each year also has a theme. In 2026 the parade marked 150 years of the song "Vande Mataram". The soldiers practise for months, starting in the cold winter mornings, until their lines are straight enough to lay a ruler along.

After the soldiers come the tableaux. Each state or ministry builds a float on a truck, often several metres tall, showing a festival, a craft, a temple or a new idea. Only some are picked each year, and states compete hard to be chosen.

Children who have won national bravery and achievement awards are part of the day too. Then motorcycle teams from the army or police ride past balanced in human pyramids, some riders standing on shoulders as the bikes move. Crowds at the side cheer louder for this than almost anything.

Watching in person takes planning. Tickets go on sale in the weeks before, and spectators arrive long before dawn, wrapped in shawls against Delhi's winter fog, because security checks take time. State capitals hold their own smaller parades, and schools across India hoist the flag and hand out sweets.

The finale belongs to the [[@indian-air-force|Indian Air Force]]. Helicopters and jets fly over in tight shapes, and fighter planes pull straight up into the sky, trailing smoke.

Each year India invites a foreign leader as chief guest. The first, in 1950, was President Sukarno of Indonesia. In 2026, for the 77th Republic Day, there were two: the presidents of the European Council and the European Commission. The celebrations close three days later at Beating Retreat, when the bands play at sunset near the government buildings on Raisina Hill and the lights come on along the buildings.

text: गालों के ज़्यादातर डिंपल एक मांसपेशी की देन हैं। जब तुम मुस्कुराते हो, तो ज़ाइगोमैटिकस मेजर नाम की मांसपेशियों की एक जोड़ी होंठों के कोनों को ऊपर गालों की हड्डियों की ओर खींचती है। कुछ लोगों में इनमें से एक मांसपेशी दो गुच्छों में बँटी होती है, या थोड़े अलग ढंग से जुड़ी होती है।

जब यह बँटी हुई मांसपेशी खिंचती है, तो दोनों गुच्छों के बीच त्वचा का एक छोटा-सा टुकड़ा भीतर की ओर खिंच जाता है। नतीजा होता है एक छोटा-सा गड्ढा, जो मुस्कुराने पर दिखता है और चेहरा ढीला पड़ते ही मिट जाता है। यही है डिंपल।

किसी का एक डिंपल पड़ता है, किसी के दो, और ज़्यादातर लोगों का एक भी नहीं। डिंपल बस चेहरों की बनावट का एक फ़र्क है, कुछ-कुछ कान के आकार जैसा। इनसे कोई नुकसान नहीं होता और इन्हें ठीक करने की ज़रूरत नहीं।

sec.t:
तुम्हारे चेहरे में 40 से ज़्यादा [[@muscles|मांसपेशियाँ]] हैं। शरीर की ज़्यादातर मांसपेशियों से अलग, इनमें से कई सिर्फ़ हड्डी से नहीं, त्वचा से भी जुड़ी होती हैं। इसीलिए तुम्हारा चेहरा इतने सारे भाव बना पाता है। ज़ाइगोमैटिकस मेजर गाल की हड्डी से होंठ के कोने तक एक तिरछी रस्सी की तरह जाती है।

चेहरों पर हुए एक छोटे अध्ययन में डॉक्टरों ने पाया कि जिन लोगों के गालों में डिंपल पड़ते थे, उनकी ज़ाइगोमैटिकस मेजर में अक्सर दो अलग-अलग पट्टियाँ थीं। जब यह कसती है, तो त्वचा दोनों पट्टियों के बीच फँस जाती है। कुछ और लोगों में [[tissue|ऊतक]] की एक छोटी पट्टी मांसपेशी को त्वचा से जोड़ती है, जिससे भी गड्ढा बन जाता है।

खुलकर हँसते समय मांसपेशी सबसे ज़ोर से खिंचती है, इसलिए जब तुम ठहाका लगाकर [[@laughter|हँसते]] हो, तब डिंपल सबसे गहरे होते हैं।

बहुत-से नन्हे बच्चों के डिंपल पड़ते हैं, जो बड़े होने पर गायब हो जाते हैं। छोटे बच्चों के गोल-मटोल गाल अपने-आप मुड़कर डिंपल बना सकते हैं। जैसे-जैसे चेहरा पतला और लंबा होता है, ये गड्ढे मिट सकते हैं। कभी-कभी उल्टा भी होता है, और बड़े बच्चे के चेहरे पर डिंपल उभर आता है।

ठुड्डी का डिंपल, यानी बीच से बँटी-सी ठुड्डी, बिल्कुल अलग चीज़ है। यह तब बनता है जब जन्म से पहले निचले जबड़े की हड्डी के दोनों आधे हिस्से पूरी तरह चिकने ढंग से नहीं जुड़ते। वहाँ एक छोटी-सी खाँच रह जाती है, और त्वचा उसी के साथ ढल जाती है।

पीठ के निचले हिस्से में भी डिंपल होते हैं। ये दो छोटे गड्ढे कूल्हों के ठीक ऊपर होते हैं, जहाँ त्वचा छोटे-छोटे [[ligament|स्नायुओं]] से नीचे की कूल्हे की हड्डी से बँधी होती है। इन्हें कभी-कभी ‘वीनस के डिंपल’ कहा जाता है।

sec.h: क्या डिंपल परिवार में चलते हैं?
sec.t:
डिंपल अक्सर माता-पिता और बच्चों, दोनों में दिखते हैं। सालों तक स्कूल की किताबें कहती रहीं कि ये एक अकेले प्रभावी [[gene|जीन]] से तय होते हैं, किसी सीधे-सादे स्विच की तरह। यह कहानी ज़रूरत से ज़्यादा सुलझी हुई है।

डिंपल वाले माता-पिता के ढेरों बच्चों के डिंपल नहीं पड़ते, और कुछ बच्चों के पड़ते हैं, जबकि माता-पिता में से किसी के नहीं होते। डिंपल सिर्फ़ एक तरफ़ भी पड़ सकता है। वैज्ञानिक अब मानते हैं कि इसमें कई [[@genes-family|जीन]] शामिल हो सकते हैं, साथ में यह भी कि जन्म से पहले चेहरा कैसे बना। बड़े, सावधानी से किए गए अध्ययन अब भी कम हैं, इसीलिए यह सवाल अभी खुला है।

डिंपल कितने आम हैं, यह इस पर निर्भर है कि किन लोगों का अध्ययन किया गया। अलग-अलग देशों के सर्वे में काफ़ी अलग-अलग अंक निकले हैं।

दुनिया के बहुत-से हिस्सों में लोगों को डिंपल प्यारे लगते हैं, और इन्हें अक्सर मिलनसार स्वभाव से जोड़ा जाता है, क्योंकि ये मुस्कान में दिखते हैं। कुछ जगहों पर लोग इन्हें बनवाने के लिए ऑपरेशन तक करवाते हैं, हालाँकि डॉक्टर याद दिलाते हैं कि बिना डिंपल वाला कुदरती चेहरा भी पूरी तरह सेहतमंद है।

चेहरे ऐसे छोटे-छोटे फ़र्कों से भरे हैं। झाइयाँ, आँखों का रंग और डिंपल हर चेहरे को इतना अनोखा बना देते हैं कि फ़ोन तक लोगों को अलग-अलग पहचान लेता है।

और सबसे अजीब बात? गोल्फ़ की गेंद पर बने छोटे-छोटे गड्ढों को भी अंग्रेज़ी में डिंपल ही कहते हैं, और ये गड्ढे विज्ञान की एक चतुर तरकीब हैं। इनसे गेंद हवा को चीरते हुए आसानी से निकलती है और लगभग दुगनी दूर उड़ती है। यह उन तरकीबों में से एक है जो [[@sports-equipment|खेल का सामान कैसे काम करता है]] में समझाई गई हैं।

text: Making AI safe and fair means checking that it works well for everyone, doesn't make dangerous mistakes, and can't easily be used to cause harm. It is less like fixing a single bug and more like the safety work done on cars or medicines: careful testing, rules, and people watching what happens once it's in use.

The problems are real today. Some programs work better for some groups of people than others. [[@chatbots|Chatbots]] sometimes state made-up facts with total confidence. And tools that create realistic pictures and voices can be used to trick people. Researchers, companies and governments are all working on fixes, and they don't always agree on the best ones.

st.prompt: A program learns to pick good job applicants from ten years of a company's past hiring. Most people hired before were men. What is likely to happen?

options.t: The program may learn to favour men, even if nobody told it to

The program will refuse to work until it gets better data

st.reveal: An AI copies the patterns in its examples. If past decisions were lopsided, it can learn the lopsidedness as if it were a rule. That's why teams test programs on many different groups before using them.

src: Buolamwini J. and Gebru T. (2018) Gender Shades. Proceedings of Machine Learning Research, vol. 81.
European Union, Artificial Intelligence Act, 2024.
n.certNote: Experts agree that today's AI can be biased and can make confident mistakes. They disagree strongly about how dangerous future AI might become and how fast, and about how much governments should regulate it.

sec.h: How a fair-looking machine becomes unfair
sec.t:
Most modern [[@ai-what|AI]] learns from examples. Show it enough photos labelled "cat" and it learns what cats look like. The same goes for faces, voices, loan applications or exam answers.

The trouble is that examples carry the habits of the past. In 2018, two researchers, Joy Buolamwini and Timnit Gebru, tested face-analysis programs from big tech companies. The programs rarely got the gender of lighter-skinned men wrong. For darker-skinned women, one program was wrong about 35% of the time. The programs had mostly been trained and tested on lighter faces.

After the study was published, several companies improved their systems. It showed something useful: you can only fix what you measure. Today, careful teams check how well a program works for people of different ages, skin colours, accents and languages before releasing it. In a country with as many languages as India, that list of checks gets long.

{{story:alan-turing}}

sec.h: When the machine is confidently wrong
sec.t:
Chatbots predict which words are likely to come next, based on huge amounts of text. That makes them fluent, but fluency is not the same as truth. Sometimes they invent a book title, a quote or a historical date that never existed. Researchers call this a hallucination.

For homework help, that's annoying. For medical or legal advice, it could be serious. So developers train chatbots to say "I'm not sure", connect them to trusted sources, and test them with thousands of tricky questions. Some teams hire people to attack their own systems on purpose, looking for weak spots before anyone else finds them. This is called red-teaming.

In 2024, the European Union passed a law that sorts AI uses by risk. Programs that score job applicants or help run power grids face strict checks. A few uses, such as scoring citizens on their behaviour, are banned. The US has taken a lighter approach so far, with some guidance from the government and laws in individual states. India has launched a national AI mission and published guidelines, and is still deciding how strict its rules should be.

Writing these [[@laws-made|laws]] is hard, because the technology changes faster than [[parliament|parliaments]] meet. Too few rules might let harm spread. Too many might slow down useful inventions, such as tools that spot disease in X-rays.

Some well-known scientists worry that much more powerful AI could one day be hard to control, and say we should prepare now. Others think those fears are exaggerated and that attention should stay on today's problems: bias, [[@fake-news|fake news]], [[@privacy|privacy]] and [[@future-jobs-ai|jobs]]. Many researchers work on both.

What nearly everyone agrees on is a simple principle. A person, not a machine, should stay responsible for important decisions about people's lives, and anyone affected should be able to ask why.

text: Alexander Graham Bell is usually named as the inventor of the telephone. A Scottish-born teacher of deaf students living in the United States, he was granted a US patent on 7 March 1876 for a way to send speech along a wire using [[@electricity-made|electricity]]. Three days later, he spoke the first clear sentence over his telephone to his assistant in the next room.

But the full story is more crowded. On the very day Bell's lawyer filed his patent application, another inventor, Elisha Gray, filed papers describing a similar idea. An Italian immigrant in New York, Antonio Meucci, had been working on a talking [[telegraph|telegraph]] for years before that. People still argue about who deserves the most credit.

st.reveal: Each phone line ran to a central exchange. You lifted the receiver, an operator answered, and you said who you wanted. She connected the call by plugging a cord into the right socket on a big switchboard. Automatic exchanges slowly replaced operators over the next century.

myth: Alexander Graham Bell invented the telephone completely on his own.

Bell received the patent and built a working telephone, but others had similar ideas. Elisha Gray filed a document about a telephone design on the same day, and Antonio Meucci had worked on a talking telegraph years earlier. Bell's assistant, Thomas Watson, also did much of the hands-on building.
facts: Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you.

sec.t:
Bell had been trying to send several [[@telegraph|telegraph]] messages along one wire at once, using different musical notes. Along the way, he became convinced that a wire could carry the rise and fall of a human [[@voice|voice]].

His telephone used a thin, flexible sheet that vibrated when someone spoke into it. The [[vibration|vibrations]] changed an electric current flowing through the wire, and at the other end, a similar sheet vibrated in the same pattern, recreating the [[@sound-travel|sound]]. On 10 March 1876, Bell spoke into his device: "Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you." Thomas Watson, listening in another room, heard him.

sec.h: A race to the patent office

sec.t:
Early telephones were sold in pairs, wired directly to each other. That quickly became impractical. Soon each phone was connected to a central exchange, where operators sat in front of switchboards and connected calls by plugging in cords.

The first telephone exchanges in India opened in 1882, in Calcutta, Bombay and Madras. For the next century, telephones were a luxury for most Indian families. In the 1980s, people often waited years for a landline connection. Then yellow STD and PCO booths spread across towns and villages, letting anyone make a long-distance call for a few rupees.

On 3 April 1973, Martin Cooper, an engineer at the company Motorola, stood on a New York street and made the first call from a handheld mobile phone. It weighed over a kilogram, about as much as a big bag of sugar. He called a rival engineer at Bell Labs to tell him.

India's first mobile phone call came on 31 July 1995, when the Chief Minister of West Bengal, Jyoti Basu, in [[@kolkata|Kolkata]], called the Union telecom minister, Sukh Ram, in Delhi. Calls were expensive at first. Within about twenty years, India had hundreds of millions of mobile users.

Today's [[@smartphones|smartphones]] are distant [[descendant|descendants]] of Bell's vibrating sheet. They still turn your voice into electrical signals, though now those signals travel as [[@radio-waves|radio waves]] and flashes of light.

text: The internet crosses oceans through cables laid on the sea floor. Inside each one are a few hair-thin strands of glass called optical fibres. Data travels along them as flashes of [[@lasers|laser]] light, millions of times a second.

More than 500 of these cables wrap the planet, linking every continent except Antarctica. Together they carry about 99% of the data travelling between continents. When you stream a video from a server in the United States to a phone in [[@kochi|Kochi]], it probably crossed the sea this way, in well under a second.

st.prompt: What damages undersea internet cables most often?

Shark bites

st.reveal: Most faults happen in shallow water near coasts, where trawlers drag nets and ships drop anchors. Earthquakes and sharks cause a few, but far fewer. Repair ships fix well over a hundred faults every year.

myth: The internet between countries travels mostly by satellite.

Satellites matter for ships, planes and remote places, but they carry only a small share of traffic. Undersea cables carry about 99% of data between continents, because they are faster and can carry far more.
facts: about the size of a garden hose

sec.h: Thin as a hose, long as a continent
sec.t:
In the deep ocean, a cable can be about as thick as a garden hose. There, kilometres down, it is safe from most dangers, so it needs little protection. Near the shore it is wrapped in layers of steel wire and buried under the sea bed, because shallow water is where the trouble is.

Light fades as it travels through glass. So every 50 to 100 km or so, a device called a repeater boosts the signal. A cable from India to Europe may have dozens of them lying on the sea floor, powered by electricity sent down the cable from land.

Special cable ships carry thousands of kilometres of cable coiled in huge tanks. Before laying starts, surveyors [[@ocean-floor-maps|map the sea floor]] to avoid cliffs, volcanoes and [[@shipwrecks|shipwrecks]]. The ship then sails slowly across the ocean, paying out cable behind it, while a plough buries it near the coast.

When a cable breaks, a repair ship sails out, hooks the broken ends with a grapnel (a kind of grappling hook), lifts them to the deck and splices in a new section. Most breaks come from fishing trawlers and ship anchors. Sharks have been seen biting cables, and some were wrapped in extra tough material, but bites cause very few faults.

Cables come ashore at buildings called landing stations. India's main ones are in Mumbai and Chennai, with others in places such as Kochi and Thoothukudi. From there, the data flows inland through fibre buried beside roads and railway lines.

In 2020 a cable of about 2,300 km opened between Chennai and the [[@andaman|Andaman and Nicobar Islands]]. Before that, the islands relied on slower satellite links. People there could suddenly stream videos and hold video lessons that had been almost impossible before.

Satellites are useful where cables can't reach, such as ships in mid-ocean or remote villages. [[@starlink|Satellite internet]] from low [[orbit|orbit]] is getting much better. But one fibre cable can carry far more data than a whole fleet of satellites, and it costs less for each bit sent. That is why companies including Google and Meta now pay to lay their own cables, threading new strands of glass across the deep sea floor where whales swim overhead.

text: In the summer of 1931, the British climber Frank Smythe and two friends were walking back from Mount Kamet when they lost their way. They came down into a high valley and found it covered in flowers, mile after mile. Smythe later wrote a book called *The Valley of Flowers*, and the name stuck.

The valley sits in the [[@himalaya-form|Himalaya]] of [[@uttarakhand|Uttarakhand]], at about 3,500 m. That is more than 1,000 m higher than the hill town of Shimla. It is now a national park and, together with nearby Nanda Devi, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. For a few weeks each [[monsoon|monsoon]], it turns pink, blue, yellow and purple.

March and April, in spring
December and January, in winter

st.reveal: Up here, spring arrives late. The snow melts in May and June, and the monsoon rain then wakes up hundreds of kinds of flowers at once. By late July and August the meadows are at their brightest.

d.try: Make a "flower count" square. Lay four pencils on a patch of grass or a garden bed to make a small square. Count how many different kinds of plants grow inside it, then try a square somewhere else and compare. Botanists use the same trick, called a quadrat, to study meadows like the Valley of Flowers.
myth: The Valley of Flowers is full of flowers all year round.
It is under snow from about November to May and closed to visitors. Flowers carpet the valley only for a short summer window, and different kinds take turns blooming between June and September.

sec.t:
No gardener has ever worked here. The valley is a [[glacier|glacier]]-carved bowl, about 8 km long, with a river called the Pushpawati running through it. *Pushpa* means flower.

Scientists have counted more than 500 kinds of higher plants in the valley. Some grow nowhere else on Earth. Look closely and you might see blue poppies, wild geraniums and cobra lilies that look like a snake about to strike. There is also the Brahma kamal, a rare white flower that is sacred in Uttarakhand.

The flowers don't all bloom together. They work in shifts. One week a slope is yellow, a few weeks later the same slope is purple, as one set of plants finishes and the next begins.

sec.h: Why so many flowers, so high up

sec.t:
In 1939, a [[botanist|botanist]] named Joan Margaret Legge came from Kew Gardens in London to study the valley's plants. While collecting flowers on a steep slope, she slipped and died. Her sister later put up a small stone memorial, and walkers still stop at her grave inside the valley today.

The park also shelters animals that are hard to spot: musk deer, Himalayan black bears, blue sheep called bharal, and the shy [[@snow-leopard|snow leopard]]. Its pugmarks have been found here, and camera traps have photographed it. Above them flies the Himalayan monal, a pheasant with feathers that shine green, blue and copper.

There is no road into the valley. Visitors drive to Govindghat, then walk or ride a mule roughly 10 to 13 km uphill to the village of Ghangaria. From there it is about 3 km more into the valley. Many of the people on the same trail are Sikh pilgrims heading to Hemkund Sahib, a gurdwara beside a glacier lake even higher up.

Nobody may camp inside the park, and visitors must leave by evening. The rules keep the meadows from being trampled. Grazing by sheep and goats was stopped in the 1980s. That caused a surprise. Some tall weeds spread fast without animals to eat them, and park staff now pull them out by hand.

From November, the snow returns and the valley disappears again, the way it has for thousands of years, long before anyone gave it a name. Snow and flowers both depend on the tilt of the Earth, which is why [[@seasons-why|the seasons]] here are so dramatic.

text: Miami is a big city near the southern tip of Florida, the sunny [[peninsula|peninsula]] that pokes down from the United States towards the Caribbean. It is warm all year, with a wet, stormy summer and a dry winter that brings tourists from colder states.

Miami is also one of the most Latin American cities in the USA. Since the 1960s, people from Cuba, Venezuela, Colombia, [[@haitian-revolution|Haiti]] and many other countries have made it home, and most people in the city speak [[@spanish-language|Spanish]] at home. It is famous for its beaches, its pastel buildings and its swampy wild neighbour, the [[@florida-everglades|Everglades]]. And because it sits so low, it is one of the American cities most worried about the rising sea.

st.prompt: Miami is building tall sea walls in places. Why can't walls alone keep the sea out?

options.t: The rock under the city is full of holes, so seawater rises up from below
Waves are too tall for any wall
Walls are not allowed on beaches in Florida

st.reveal: Most of South Florida sits on limestone, a rock riddled with holes like a sponge. When the sea rises, water seeps sideways and upwards through the ground. That is why engineers are also raising roads and installing pumps.

myth: The Everglades is just a big, still swamp.
The Everglades is a very wide, very shallow river. Its water flows slowly south through sawgrass towards the sea, which is why the writer Marjory Stoneman Douglas called it a "river of grass".

sec.h: A city built by a railway
sec.t:
In the early 1890s, Miami was little more than a trading post. A widow named Julia Tuttle owned land by the Miami River and wanted a city there. She persuaded the businessman Henry Flagler to bring his railway south. The trains arrived in 1896 and the city was founded the same year. Julia Tuttle is often called the mother of Miami.

The railway brought builders, hotels and holidaymakers. In the 1920s and 1930s, Miami Beach filled with Art Deco hotels painted pink, mint and lemon, with curved corners and porthole windows that look a little like ships.

Much of Miami is only about 2 metres above sea level. During the highest tides of the year, called king tides, water can bubble out of drains and cover streets even when no rain falls. In Miami Beach, the city has raised some roads and installed pumps to push the water back out.

The rock under South Florida makes this hard. It is limestone, full of tiny holes, so seawater soaks through the ground rather than over a wall. Scientists expect [[@sea-level-rise|sea level rise]] to make these floods more frequent in the coming decades. Miami also sits in the path of [[@hurricanes|hurricanes]]. [[hurricane|Hurricane]] Andrew in 1992 flattened tens of thousands of homes south of the city.

West of Miami lies the Everglades, a vast, shallow sheet of water flowing south through sawgrass taller than a child. Everglades National Park was set up in 1947 to protect part of it. The US National Park Service says it is the only place in the world where alligators and crocodiles live side by side.

Canals and farms have drained much of the old Everglades, and engineers are now trying to restore the natural flow. Miami gets most of its drinking water from the ground beneath this [[@wetlands|wetland]], so keeping it wet matters for more than wading birds. It keeps the taps running.

text: Russia is the biggest country in the world by far. It covers about 17 million square kilometres, roughly one-ninth of all the land on Earth. It is more than five times the size of India and almost twice the size of the United States.

It stretches across two continents. The Ural Mountains divide European Russia, in the west, from Asian Russia, called Siberia, in the east. Most Russians live in the European part, around cities like Moscow and Saint Petersburg. Siberia is enormous but thinly populated, with vast forests, frozen ground and rivers longer than [[@rivers-himalaya|the Ganga]].

st.prompt: Russia stretches across Europe and Asia. How many time zones does it have?

options.t: Eleven
Three
Twenty-four

st.reveal: Russia uses eleven time zones, more than any other single block of land. When it is 9 am in Kaliningrad in the west, it is 7 pm in Kamchatka in the far east.

myth: It is freezing cold everywhere in Russia, all year round.
Winters are long and cold, especially in Siberia, but Moscow often reaches 25 to 30 °C in summer. The southern resort of Sochi, on the Black Sea, has palm trees and warm beaches.
facts: about 17 million sq km, the largest country on Earth

sec.t:
From the Baltic Sea in the west to the Pacific Ocean in the east, Russia is about 9,000 km wide. When the Sun rises over the Pacific coast, it is still the middle of the previous evening in the west.

So Russia uses eleven time zones. If you could speak to friends in [[@puzzle-konigsberg|Kaliningrad]], in the far west, and Kamchatka, in the far east, at the same moment, one would be having breakfast and the other dinner.

The Trans-Siberian Railway links Moscow with Vladivostok, on the Pacific coast. The main route is over 9,000 km long, the longest railway line in the world. A non-stop journey takes about a week and crosses seven or eight time zones, depending on the route.

Passengers sleep in bunks, drink tea from hot-water boilers at the end of each carriage, and buy snacks from people selling food on station platforms. Outside the window, the birch and pine forests of Siberia, called the taiga, roll past for days.

Lake Baikal, in southern Siberia, is the deepest lake on Earth, at about 1,640 m. It is also among the oldest, around 25 million years old. It holds so much water that if every river on Earth emptied into it, they would take more than half a year to fill it.

Baikal is home to animals found nowhere else, including the nerpa, one of the few seals in the world that live only in fresh water. In winter, the lake freezes so thick that people drive across it on marked ice roads.

In 1957, the Soviet Union, of which Russia was the largest part, launched Sputnik, the first artificial satellite. In 1961, Yuri Gagarin became the first person in space, a story told in [[@first-in-space|the first person in space]]. In 1984, Rakesh Sharma became the first Indian in space, flying aboard a Soviet Soyuz spacecraft.

Russia is famous for its writers, such as Leo Tolstoy, and for composers like Tchaikovsky, who wrote the music for the ballets [[@ballet|Swan Lake]] and The Nutcracker. Moscow's Red Square, with the colourful onion domes of Saint Basil's Cathedral, is one of the best-known sights on Earth.

text: Uluru is a giant sandstone rock in the middle of Australia's Northern Territory, about 450 km by road from the town of Alice Springs. It stands 348 m above the flat desert around it, a little taller than the [[@eiffel-visit|Eiffel Tower]]. Walking all the way round its base is about 9.4 km and takes most people three to four hours.

To scientists, Uluru is the tip of an ancient rock layer pushed up on its edge. To the Anangu, the Aboriginal people whose land it is, Uluru is a sacred place full of stories, laws and ancestors. Both ways of seeing it shape how the rock is looked after today.

st.prompt: Uluru looks deep red, but break off a fresh piece (which you are not allowed to do) and it is greyish. Why is the outside red?

options.t: Iron in the rock has rusted where it meets the air
Red desert dust has been glued on by rain
Lichens growing on the rock are red

st.reveal: The rock contains iron-bearing minerals. Where air and rain touch the surface, the iron slowly rusts, giving the rock a thin orange-red skin. In caves and cracks where the weather can't reach, the stone is grey.

d.try: Leave an iron nail or a steel wool pad (ask an adult) in a saucer with a little water for a few days. Watch it turn orange. That is the same chemistry that paints Uluru red, only far faster.
myth: Uluru is the biggest single rock in the world.

Mount Augustus in Western Australia is often said to be more than twice as large. Geologists also point out that Uluru is not a lone boulder. It is the top of a huge tilted layer of rock that continues deep underground.

sec.h: A rock standing on its edge

sec.t:
The rock's red skin is [[@rust|rust]], a thin coating on the surface of the stone. Iron in its minerals reacts with oxygen and water, just as an old bicycle chain does. Freshly broken rock from inside is grey.

At sunrise and sunset, sunlight passes through more of the [[atmosphere|atmosphere]], and the blue light is scattered away. Only orange and red light reach the rock, so Uluru seems to glow and change shade by the minute. That is the same reason the [[@colour-of-sky-sunset|sky turns red at sunset]]. After rare heavy rain, the rock turns silvery and waterfalls pour off its sides.

Aboriginal people have lived in this part of Australia for tens of thousands of years. For the Anangu, Uluru is part of Tjukurpa, the knowledge that explains how the world was made and how people should live. Caves around its base hold old paintings. Some places on the rock are so sacred that visitors are asked not to photograph them. Anangu rangers lead walks around the base, pointing out plants used for food and medicine. At the foot of the rock, the Mutitjulu waterhole holds water for much of the year and has long drawn people and animals.

In 1873, an English surveyor named William Gosse saw the rock and called it Ayers Rock, after a South Australian politician. For about a century that was its official name. In 1993 it got a double name, Ayers Rock / Uluru. In 2002 the order was swapped, and today almost everyone simply calls it Uluru.

On 26 October 1985, the Australian government handed the land back to the Anangu. They leased it to the national parks service, and the two now run the park together.

For decades, tourists climbed a steep path to the top, holding a chain. The Anangu asked people not to, because the route follows a sacred path, and because dozens of climbers had died in falls or from heat. On 26 October 2019, exactly 34 years after the handback, the climb closed for good.

The park's other famous sight is Kata Tjuta, a cluster of 36 rounded domes about 25 km away. Like Uluru, it is sacred, and like the [[@deserts-world|deserts of the world]] around it, it can swing from freezing nights to scorching afternoons in a single day.

text: Momos are small dumplings, a wrapper of thin dough folded around a filling, usually steamed. They come from Tibet and Nepal, where they were warm, filling food for cold mountain days. Families in Sikkim, Darjeeling, Ladakh and the Northeast have eaten them for generations.

From the 1960s onwards, Tibetan [[refugee|refugees]] and Nepali and Northeastern families settled in cities across India. Many opened small eateries and street stalls. Momos were cheap, quick and tasty, and they spread like wildfire, especially in Delhi.
Today they are a street-food staple from Kolkata to Bengaluru, and among the most-ordered snacks on food delivery apps.

st.prompt: Why are classic momos steamed rather than boiled in water?

options.t: Steam cooks them without making the thin wrapper soggy or split
Steam is much hotter than boiling water
Boiling would make the filling sweet

st.reveal: Steam cooks the dough and filling gently and evenly while keeping the juices sealed inside. In boiling water the thin wrapper soaks up liquid, and a weak seal can burst open.

n.certNote: Food historians agree momos came to India from Tibet and Nepal, but exactly when and through which route they first arrived is not well recorded. Many families and towns tell their own versions.

d.try: Fold paper momos. Cut circles from paper about the size of your palm, put a cotton ball in the middle as "filling", and try pleating the edges together into a pouch or a half-moon. Count how many pleats you can make. Skilled momo makers often do a dozen or more in seconds.
myth: The MSG (ajinomoto) used in some momos and chutneys is harmful to eat.
Food safety agencies such as the US FDA say MSG is safe at normal amounts. It is made from glutamate, the same substance that gives tomatoes, cheese and mushrooms their savoury taste.

sec.t:
In Tibet, where few vegetables grow, momos were traditionally filled with yak meat or mutton, seasoned with onion, garlic and ginger. They were steamed in stacked metal trays over a pot of boiling water. In the thin air of the plateau, at over 4,000 metres, water boils at only about 86°C, so steaming was a gentle, fuel-saving way to cook. Fuel was precious, often dried yak dung.

Newar traders from the Kathmandu valley, who travelled to Lhasa for centuries, are often credited with bringing momos to Nepal. There, people adapted them with buffalo meat, local spices and a fiery tomato pickle called achar.

The name itself has travelled too. Many experts think "momo" comes from a Chinese word for a steamed bun, which passed into Tibetan before reaching the rest of South Asia.

sec.h: How momos came down the mountains

sec.t:
Once momos reached the plains, cooks began to play. Vegetarian momos filled with cabbage, carrot and paneer appeared for families who did not eat meat. Then came fried momos, crunchy kurkure momos coated in cornflakes, and tandoori momos marinated in spiced yoghurt and grilled in a clay oven.

The chutney changed too. The bright red, garlicky chilli dip served with Delhi momos is hotter than many traditional Tibetan sauces. In Nepal, people love jhol momo, served floating in a tangy, soupy sauce.

Chefs have even made chocolate momos and cheesy pizza momos. In Ladakh and Sikkim, many people still prefer them the old way, plain and juicy, with a bowl of thukpa noodle soup on the side. Not everyone approves, but it shows how a dish becomes local: people cook it their own way.

Wrapping a filling in dough and cooking it is one of humanity's favourite food ideas. China has jiaozi and dim sum. Japan has gyoza. Turkey and Central Asia have tiny manti. Poland has pierogi. Italy has ravioli. India has its own too, like sweet modaks and Gujarati ghughra.

That savoury, mouth-watering taste in a good meaty momo has a name: [[@food-science-umami|umami]]. It is the same taste found in tomatoes, mushrooms and cheese, and scientists only agreed it was a real basic taste in the late twentieth century. Its story begins with a Japanese chemist and a bowl of seaweed soup.

text: Almost every city on Earth has its own street food, cheap snacks and meals cooked and sold on pavements, carts and stalls. India has [[@pani-puri|pani puri]], vada pav and chaat. Mexico has [[@tacos|tacos]]. Vietnam has bánh mì sandwiches, Japan has takoyaki, Turkey has sesame-crusted simit, and New York has hot dogs and pretzels.

Many street foods tell stories of travel. Recipes moved with traders, workers and rulers, and street cooks mixed them with local tastes. People love them because they are fast, filling and full of flavour, and because eating standing up beside strangers is part of the fun.

st.prompt: Vietnam's famous bánh mì sandwich uses which kind of bread?

options.t: A French-style baguette
A flat Indian roti
A Japanese steamed bun

st.reveal: France ruled Vietnam for decades and brought the baguette. Vietnamese bakers made it lighter and crispier, and street cooks filled it with pickled vegetables, herbs, chillies and meat or tofu. The bread is French, but the taste is Vietnamese.

d.try: Plan a "street food world tour" at home with an adult. Pick two easy street snacks from different countries, like a simple chaat and a cucumber bánh mì-style sandwich. Make them together and score each for sweet, sour, salty, spicy and crunchy.
myth: Street food is always unsafe to eat.

Plenty of street food is cooked fresh in front of you at high heat, which kills most germs. Busy stalls with quick turnover, clean water and hot food are usually a good sign. As anywhere, care with uncooked food and water makes sense.

sec.t:
India has an enormous range of street snacks, changing every few hundred kilometres. In [[@mumbai|Mumbai]], the vada pav, a spicy potato fritter in a soft bun, is often traced to the 1960s, when stalls near train stations sold it to mill workers. Kolkata's kathi roll started as kebabs wrapped in paratha so office workers could eat without greasy fingers.

The same crispy shell filled with spicy water is called pani puri in Mumbai, golgappa in Delhi and puchka in Kolkata. In Indore, Sarafa Bazaar is a jewellery market by day and turns into a busy food street at night.

[[@singapore|Singapore]] moved its street sellers into hawker centres from the 1970s, open-air food courts with dozens of stalls. In 2020, UNESCO added Singapore's hawker culture to its list of world cultural traditions. Some hawker stalls have even won Michelin stars.

In Japan, takoyaki is a ball of batter with a piece of octopus inside, cooked in a special pan with round dips. It was first sold in Osaka in the 1930s. In Taiwan, night markets sell bubble tea, which was invented there in the 1980s. In Bangkok, stalls sell noodle soups, grilled meat on sticks and mango sticky rice late into the night.

Vietnam's bánh mì shows how history ends up in food. French rulers brought the baguette in the 1800s. Vietnamese cooks made it lighter and filled it with pickled carrots, coriander, chillies and pâté or tofu.

In Turkey, sellers carry stacks of simit, sesame bread rings, on trays balanced on their heads. In China, steamed baozi buns are a common breakfast eaten on the go.

In New York City, carts sell hot dogs, pretzels and halal chicken and rice. Food trucks became a big trend in the late 2000s, when a truck in Los Angeles started selling Korean barbecue tacos and announced its location online. Hot dog carts spread in New York in the late 1800s, many run by German immigrants. Soft pretzels arrived with German settlers too, and they are still a famous snack in Philadelphia.

Behind every stall is someone who wakes before dawn to chop, fry and haul their cart into place. Millions of [[@people-street-vendors|street vendors]] in India earn their living this way. And the strangest part? Many dishes now served in fancy restaurants, from pani puri shots to gourmet tacos, began as cheap snacks on a pavement corner.
